questions.q: Who is the protagonist of "ल्वज्न्कल ध >कसैम+ह" and what is the central conflict he faces?
questions.a: The protagonist is ल्वज्न्कल, an elderly man whose son and daughter-in-law force him out of his own house; his central conflict is the struggle to retain his dignity and identity after being dispossessed of the home that holds his life's memories. A wrong answer (e.g., naming the son txèkj as protagonist) reveals the student cannot distinguish the central consciousness around which the narrative revolves from the antagonist who drives the external conflict.

questions.q: In your own words, explain why ल्वज्न्कल refuses to leave the threshold (देहलीज़) even when his son and daughter-in-law try to force him out.
questions.a: ल्वज्न्कल refuses to leave because the threshold is the physical anchor of his entire existence — it holds his wife's ashes (अस्थि), the memories of his children's upbringing, and the labour of his lifetime; leaving would mean accepting that his identity can be erased by others' cruelty. A wrong answer focusing only on physical comfort or stubbornness shows the student misses the symbolic weight of the threshold as the site where memory, identity, and resistance intersect.

questions.q: Using the PEEL structure, write a 4-sentence paragraph analyzing ल्वज्न्कल's dignity in the final scene where he builds a new house.
questions.a: **Point:** ल्वज्न्कल's act of building a new house reclaims his agency. **Evidence:** The text shows him "ज्क्क ड्क्सज ध <सज ड्क्स नक्सुकसा ग्क्कक्सा ल्स म्म+कुस यक्स" (he pushed the roof beams with both hands toward the sky). **Explanation:** This physical labour, done alone and without bitterness, transforms his victimhood into creative resistance — he builds not to spite his son but to prove his self-worth. **Link:** Thus the new house becomes a metaphor for dignity that cannot be demolished by familial betrayal. A wrong answer that merely narrates "he built a house" without the explanatory link to agency and theme shows inability to move from plot summary to character analysis.

questions.q: Compare ल्वज्न्कल's response to injustice with a typical "rebellious" protagonist in social realism. What does his non-violent, constructive resistance reveal about the author's view on elderly agency?
questions.a: Unlike a rebellious protagonist who might confront or sue, ल्वज्न्कल chooses silent rebuilding — his resistance is generative, not destructive. This reveals the author's view that elderly agency lies not in retaliation but in the quiet power to recreate one's world, affirming that dignity is an internal resource no external force can confiscate. A wrong answer calling him "passive" or "weak" fails to distinguish between passivity (inaction) and strategic non-violence (purposeful constructive action).

questions.q: Critique the statement: "ल्वज्न्कल is a helpless victim of circumstances with no control over his fate." Support your judgment with textual evidence.
questions.a: The statement is partially true for the middle section (he is physically forced out) but false for the narrative arc as a whole. Evidence: his final words "रक्स गे ल्कस य्क्क क्क्ज क्क्ज कुक,ीक्स" (then we too will build many times over) and the action of building demonstrate reclaimed control. The author structures the story to move from victimhood to agency, making the critique that he "has no control" valid only if one stops reading before the last two pages. A wrong answer that agrees entirely ignores the structural turning point where the protagonist becomes the architect of his own resolution.

questions.q: Write a diary entry from ल्वज्न्कल's perspective on the night he is forced out, using at least three key Hindi words from the text (e.g., इकस्यह, व्क्स, ब्ज़;क्ज़) to capture his inner voice.
questions.a: A strong entry uses first-person voice, incorporates the specified vocabulary naturally (e.g., "आज मेरी इकस्यह उजड़ गई, व्क्स ऐसी कि... पर ब्ज़;क्ज़ कहती है हार नहीं माननी"), shows emotional progression from grief to resolve, and avoids modern anachronisms. A weak entry writes in third person, uses generic Hindi ("दुखी हूँ") without textual vocabulary, or turns the diary into a plot summary without interiority.
